title: Sowing peas
subtitle: A successional sowing schedule for fresh peas from June to August
excerpt: Peas are sown direct from February to June in the UK, with the earliest sowings going into cold soil under fleece. Two or three small sowings three weeks apart give a longer harvest window than one large sowing.
sourceNotes: Mrs Beeton, Book of Household Management (1861), chapter on kitchen garden. RHS pea growing guide (rhs.org.uk). USDA agricultural extension service notes on pea sowing schedules and inoculation, public domain.

glossaryTerms.definition: Making two or three small sowings at intervals of two to three weeks, rather than one large sowing. The result is a spread of harvest dates rather than a single glut. For peas, two rows sown three weeks apart gives eight to ten weeks of picking rather than three to four.

Treating pea and bean seeds with rhizobium bacteria before sowing. The bacteria colonise the plant roots and fix atmospheric nitrogen, reducing or eliminating the need for nitrogen fertiliser. The inoculant is available as a powder that the seeds are dusted with before sowing. Most UK garden soils already carry sufficient rhizobium from previous legume crops.

content.text: Peas are sown direct into the ground from February through to early June in the UK, with the first sowings going into cold soil and needing fleece to get moving. A short row sown every three weeks gives fresh peas from late June through to August without a glut. The seed is large and easy to handle; germination is reliable when the soil is above 5°C.

Late February is the earliest outdoor sowing date for most of the UK, with fleece laid over the row. Without fleece, wait until mid-March in the south and April in the north. The last sensible sowing date is early June: after that the plants will be harvestable only in September and will be fighting powdery mildew by August. Three sowings in March, April, and May is the standard

Peas need full sun and a well-drained, reasonably fertile soil. Heavy clay suits them less well than a lighter loam. They fix their own nitrogen so they don't need a rich manured bed; a bed that's had brassicas or roots previously works well. Avoid sowing peas where you grew peas or beans in the last two years.

Draw a flat-bottomed drill 5 cm deep and 20 cm wide using a hoe or the back of a trowel. Sow seeds 5 cm apart in a double or triple row across the width of the drill. This gives a dense productive row rather than a thin single line. Cover, firm gently, water if dry. Net immediately against birds and mice, both will excavate the seeds within hours of sowing.

Germination takes seven to fourteen days at 10-15°C and four to seven days when the soil is warmer. The seedling emerges as a single shoot with the first pair of leaves. Mice take seeds underground and leave no trace; an empty row with no surface disturbance usually means mice rather than germination failure. Reset traps immediately.

Put in pea sticks or netting once the seedlings are 5 cm tall. Twiggy pea sticks (hazel, birch, or any woody prunings) pushed in along each side of the row are the traditional method; the plants grab on and the screen looks good. Proprietary pea netting on canes works well too. Unsupported peas flop and pod where slugs can reach them.

Water once the pods form, not before. Peas on a light soil in a dry April may need a drink; otherwise they manage on rainfall. A good water when you see pods swelling improves the fill. Remove all plants and their roots after harvest; the roots carry the nitrogen-fixing nodules, so leave them chopped in as green manure rather than composting them. attrs.heading: Common problems
attrs.intro: The main things that go wrong with peas, and what to do.

items.symptom: Seeds eaten underground, no seedlings appear
items.cause: Mice. They locate seed by smell and dig directly to it.
items.fix: Set mouse traps along the row before sowing. Remove the traps once seedlings are 5 cm tall. Covering the row with fine mesh for the first ten days also works.

items.symptom: Powdery white coating on leaves in late summer
items.cause: Powdery mildew, a fungal disease favoured by warm dry weather.
items.fix: Remove and compost affected plants. Do not sow peas after early June to avoid the late-season mildew window. Choose mildew-resistant varieties such as Alderman or Feltham First for late sowings.

items.symptom: Plants flower but pods stay short and empty
items.cause: Pea moth caterpillars inside the pods, or drought stress at pod-set.
items.fix: Cover the plants with fine mesh (insect-proof netting) from flower onset through to harvest to exclude pea moth. Water at pod-set if there has been no rain for more than a week.

items.symptom: Plants turn yellow and fail before fruiting
items.cause: Root rot, usually from poorly drained cold soil combined with wet conditions.
items.fix: Improve drainage before next sowing. Delay sowing until the soil has dried and warmed. Don't sow into cold wet ground before mid-March without protection.
